title: ReefNet: A Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for Fine-Grained Coral Reef Recognition
claim: A benchmark combines multi-source data with a split, adaptation regimes and two test sets that together define the evaluation protocol.
layout: 2 panels, left dataset then right protocol flowing top-down, converging arrows
description: The figure has two panels under blue gradient headers. The left panel, 'ReefNet Dataset', shows yellow labels for 76 CoralNet sources and Al-Wajh (Red Sea). Under them are a cartoon coral icon and a map of the Red Sea region, then a world map with yellow dots for geographic coverage. Below the maps are key statistics (~925K annotations, 479,027 filtered points, 39 labels) and a three-step taxonomy chain from Order to Family to Label in deepening salmon boxes. The right panel, 'Benchmark tasks for coral recognition', runs top-down. It starts with a Train/Validation/Test split with coral photo thumbnails. Next come three dark-teal adaptation boxes: zero-shot, few-shot and full fine-tuning. Arrows merge them into an evaluation step that branches into within-source ReefNet and cross-source Al-Wajh results, each with photos and caveat footnotes.
caption: ReefNet benchmark overview. All crops from one original image share a split. Adaptation uses ReefNet training points and validation-based selection; zero-shot models use no ReefNet training examples. Every regime is evaluated on both test sets. Al-Wajh never enters training or selection; its metric averages over 13 present genera. The standard protocol retains 39 output labels; Claude/GPT API prompts instead list 13 Al-Wajh candidates. Photos illustrate the protocol and do not identify actual split membership.
abstract: Coral reef monitoring requires scalable recognition of visually similar taxa across heterogeneous underwater surveys. We introduce ReefNet, a public dataset that aligns approximately 925K hard-coral point annotations from 76 CoralNet sources and an independently collected Al-Wajh dataset with the World Register of Marine Species taxonomy. A stratified expert audit of 8,962 patches guides filtering to a 479,027-annotation benchmark with 39 labels: 38 genera and the family Fungiidae. Expert agreement is 92% on the retained audit subset, rather than an exhaustive accuracy estimate. We evaluate pretrained models through zero-shot recognition, few-shot adaptation, and full fine-tuning, each on within-source ReefNet and held-out-source Al-Wajh tests. Biological vision-language pretraining provides the strongest zero-shot results; supervised adaptation substantially improves recognition, with DINOv2 reaching 65.79% macro recall on Al-Wajh. Matched text-description experiments improve all four evaluated MLLMs on Al-Wajh, while a GPT-5.4 reasoning ablation does not improve over direct classification. Long-tail recognition, label uncertainty, and geographic imbalance remain challenges. ReefNet provides a taxonomically grounded resource for studying these challenges; the Al-Wajh test is a regional stress test rather than evidence of global robustness. Public data and resource links are documented in the supplement.
